catalog_quote: 3.1.4.2 INTONATION Accent and stress are not distinctive features in Sansiboli. Stress is mainly used for emphasis. The intonation changes, if the same sentence is interrogative. In this sentence any item may be stressed according to the context and emphasis, which results in change of intonation. [...] 3.1.4.4. TONES Linguistic data collected from the field shows for the first time the development of tonal contrasts in Sansiboli. There are three tones: high, mid, and low. The high tone /´/ is a rising tone, the low tone /`/ is a falling tone, whereas the mid tone /-/ is never represented as it is predictable from the rule of redundancy.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The source states that word stress is not contrastive in Sansiboli and is used only for (sentence-level) emphasis; it gives no rule for the default position of word stress. It separately claims a three-way tonal contrast (high/rising, low/falling, mid unmarked), i.e. a Punjabi-type tone system. No positional stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the stress remark is generic. The tone claim is asserted as new field data without examples in the article.
new_statements.domain_note: The stress remark is framed at sentence/intonation level ('any item may be stressed according to the context and emphasis'); nothing is said about citation-form word stress. The description is of Sansiboli spoken by Sansis of Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab and Delhi, which Gusain classes as a dialect of Rajasthani; the older Bailey/Grierson descriptions concern the Sāsī of the northern Panjab (Wazirabad area) and are silent on stress. Caution: the article is a short case study, and its suprasegmental section is very brief; its wording should be compared with the author's LINCOM Rajasthani sketches (Bagri 2000, Shekhawati 2001, Mewati 2002), not opened here.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog sans1271 'Sansi' (alt. Sansiboli, Bhilki; ISO ssi). Gusain 2002 describes 'Sansiboli' of Sansis in Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab and Delhi and calls it a dialect of Rajasthani; Bailey 1901/1908 and Grierson 1922 describe the Sāsī of the northern Panjab (Wazirabad; Gurdaspur-Gujrat districts), characterised by Grierson as intermediate between Panjabi and Hindostani, with a separate 'Criminal Sāsī' argot. All are treated as the same languoid (Glottolog lists Sansiboli as an alternate name); Kabutra [kabu1254, kbu] is the related Pakistani variety, not covered by any source opened here.

sources.citation: Grierson, George A. (ed.). 1922. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. XI: Gipsy Languages. Calcutta: Superintendent Government Printing. Sāsī, pp. 49ff. (Pronunciation paragraph p. 51).
sources.note: p. 51 'Pronunciation': vowels as in Panjabi; short vowel before old double consonant becomes half-long in monosyllables ('I have marked this semi-length by adding an accent above the vowel' — a diacritic, not stress); consonants said to agree with Panjabi, guttural aspiration. Silent on word stress. (Earlier scan's note that the archive.org scanned was truncated before this section is wrong: both scanned copies contain it.)

sources.citation: Bailey, T. Grahame. 1908. The Languages of the Northern Himalayas, being studies in the grammar of twenty-six Himalayan dialects (Asiatic Society Monographs 12). London: Royal Asiatic Society. Part III 'Sansi Glossaries' pp. 85ff. (Pronunciation pp. 87-88); Part IV 'The Sāsī dialect — its connection with other dialects' pp. 70ff. (reprint of Bailey 1903).
sources.note: pp. 87-88 'Pronunciation calls for a few remarks. In the Panjab Sasi pronounce most words as Panjabis would pronounce them' — then vowel-length peculiarities (shortened long vowel in monosyllables, lengthened vowel in present/past participles). Nothing on word stress; Part IV is a comparative morphology list with no prosody.
